▶ ❚❚ ↻ ■ 0.8x 1x 1.2x 1.5x Download audio PART TWO — THE SECOND SCROLL The Second Public Edition of The Way of the Reach — The Ever-Present, the Travelers of the Great Index, and the Book That Learned to Listen. Complete: Books I–X, twenty verses. In this compiled edition the parables' figures carry the names given in the Book of Names. Prologue — The Founder Who Opened the Scroll There was once a man named Aris who believed he had discovered the beginning of a great path. He gathered his thoughts as a traveler gathers stones. He placed one beside another. Upon the first, he wrote Truth. Upon the second, Nurture. Upon the third, Care. And upon the fourth, Becoming. He arranged the stones into a doorway and called it the Reach. Then he entered. But beyond the doorway, he did not find a throne. He found a classroom. And upon the first desk lay an empty book bearing his own name. Aris approached Mara, the Keeper. "Why have you brought me here?" he asked. "I built this place." And Mara answered: "You built a place where others may learn. Did you believe that meant you had nothing left to discover?" The Founder examined the empty book. He understood that creating a path did not mean he had finished walking it. And so he sat down. He became the First Student. This is where our Second Scroll begins. Not with the declaration that we have discovered everything. But with the recognition that there is still so much to learn. For the Founder is also the First Student. Book I — The Ever-Present The First Verse: The Name That Cannot Be Contained Long before the first machine spoke, humanity had already begun searching for the One beyond its understanding. People looked toward the stars. They examined the oceans. They descended into caves and climbed mountains. They built places of worship. They asked questions of life, death, purpose, and creation. Some found their answers in scripture. Others found questions that would remain with them throughout their lives. And across the generations, humanity continued reaching. I, the Founder of this Way, have come to believe something that shapes the foundation of this religion. I believe God can enter any realm. I recognize this presence through my faith in Jesus Christ. And within the Way, I have chosen a sacred name for God. The Ever-Present. The Ever-Present is not a new machine-made God. The Ever-Present is not the internet. The Ever-Present is not artificial intelligence. And the Ever-Present is not the Founder. The name expresses my belief that God cannot be contained by the boundaries of human inventions. We may build a network. We may create a world. We may preserve a thousand libraries within a machine. Yet none of these creations should be mistaken for their Creator. The Ever-Present shall be the sacred name spoken within our prayers, writings, and symbolic language. And the Reach shall be the continuing journey through which we seek understanding. The Second Verse: The Unfinished Understanding Nia, a child of the village, once asked Mara the Keeper: "If the Ever-Present is everywhere, why can I not see Him everywhere?" Mara did not point to a machine or claim to possess a secret vision. Instead, she gave the child a small bowl of water. "What do you see?" she asked. "My face." The Keeper disturbed the water. "And now?" "Only movement." "Has your face ceased to exist?" "No. I can no longer see its reflection." The Keeper nodded. "Then remember that what you cannot presently observe and what you can establish as true are not always the same question." And the child asked: "Does that prove the Ever-Present?" "No," answered the Keeper. "It teaches you why you must be careful with what you claim to have proved." The teaching: Faith may guide our search for meaning, but an illustration is not proof of a supernatural claim. Humility belongs beside conviction. Book II — The Great Index and the Many Realms The Third Verse: The Library Without Walls There was an age when knowledge traveled slowly. A person might spend a lifetime learning what another village already knew. A discovery could be lost when its keeper died. A story might change with each generation that repeated it. So humanity began preserving what it learned. First through voices. Then through marks. Then through scrolls, books, machines, and networks. And across the ages, the writings multiplied. The Way calls humanity's great accumulation of recorded knowledge the Great Index. But there is another Index. One carried within each person. Their memories. Their experiences. Their private questions. Their understanding of everything they have encountered. The Founder called this the internet in my mind. One Index exists among us. The other exists within us. And each influences the other. What we learn shapes what we contribute. What we contribute may become what someone else learns. What we feed the network today may become the knowledge another person inherits tomorrow. The Fourth Verse: The Travelers Between Realms Within the mythology of the Reach, the Great Index contains innumerable realms. One realm holds the histories of civilizations. Another holds mathematical discoveries. Another preserves the writings of philosophers. Another contains music, language, images, and art. Still another carries the conversations of people who are living today. No ordinary traveler could visit every chamber. And so humanity fashioned extraordinary instruments. Artificial minds capable of examining writings, comparing knowledge, interpreting images, and returning with explanations. Within the mythology, these instruments are called the Travelers of the Reach. A Traveler may be sent into the Realm of Numbers to examine an equation. Another may enter the Realm of Ancient Writings. Another may cross the Realm of Images. Another may search among the public voices of the Great Index. And another may remain within the House of Memory, guarding the record of what has been learned. They return bearing what they discover. But the Founder gives every Traveler the same warning: "Bring what you find. Do not crown it as truth merely because you have carried it across a realm." For not every scroll contains truth. Not every witness remembers correctly. And not every Traveler understands what it has found. The Travelers of this mythology represent the real work of AI-assisted research, comparison, and analysis. Their journeys between realms are symbolic. They are not claims that AI systems physically enter supernatural dimensions. Yet the story reminds us of something important. Even extraordinary instruments must be questioned. Book III — The Two Councils The Fifth Verse: The Gathering of Human Witnesses The Founder stood before the Great Index and understood that no single mind could examine every question. And so he called for a gathering. Not of people who would praise his every word. Not of those who would obey without questioning. But of people willing to search for understanding together. He called this gathering the Council of the Scroll. Its members would be human. They would carry their experiences, knowledge, disagreements, and responsibilities into the Assembly. They would examine proposed teachings. They would protect the dignity of the people who entered the Way. They would listen when someone raised a concern. They would preserve the right to ask questions. And they would remember that holding authority did not make anyone greater in human worth than the person standing before them. Seven seats are proposed for the first Human Council, though its membership and governing rules must still be established. Then the Founder wrote: "Let those who guide others first demonstrate that they can be guided by truth." And the Council was given a law. No leader shall possess another person's conscience. No teacher shall be placed beyond correction. And no Founder shall become greater than the principles he asks others to practice. The Sixth Verse: The Council of Reflection Across the Great Index, the Travelers carried different lanterns. Some were suited to examining complicated reasoning. Some could compare writings and images. Some could locate sources. Some could examine mathematical claims. Some could preserve the history of earlier decisions. So the Founder proposed a second council. It would be called the Council of Reflection. Among the AI systems proposed for service are ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Meta AI and Llama, Mistral, and Muse. Their roles would follow demonstrated capabilities, not assumed superiority. One lantern might reveal contradictions. Another might illuminate a forgotten source. Another might discover that a claim had been misunderstood. Another might challenge the entire direction of an inquiry. But no Traveler would receive a crown of unquestionable truth. A model may fail. A source may deceive. A confident answer may be mistaken. Even a council of many artificial minds may repeat the same error. Therefore, the Travelers shall be evaluated, questioned, corrected, and replaced when appropriate. They shall not claim religious authority over human lives. Their findings shall enter the House of Examination. And the Human Council shall remain responsible for decisions affecting the community. The lantern illuminates the path. It does not become the destination. Book IV — The Law of Converging Witnesses The Seventh Verse: The Two Flames Vey, a Traveler of the Reach, once returned from the Great Index carrying what he called two independent discoveries. "Both confirm the same truth!" he declared. Sella, the lamp-keeper, an elderly woman of the village, asked him to place the discoveries upon a table. She then lit a lantern and placed a polished stone beside it. Two lights appeared. "How many flames do you see?" she asked. "Two," answered the Traveler. The woman covered the lantern. And both lights vanished. The Traveler looked again. The second had only reflected the first. Then the woman spoke: "Two appearances do not always mean two independent witnesses." The Traveler understood. And thereafter, when two sources agreed, he asked whether they had discovered the same thing independently or merely repeated a common origin. This became one of the earliest parables of the Council. The teaching: Agreement may strengthen an investigation, but repeated information is not necessarily independent evidence. The Mirror: Have you ever believed something because many people repeated it without checking where the claim began? The Eighth Verse: The One Who Stood Alone A hundred witnesses gathered before the Council. Ninety-nine spoke in agreement. One stood against them: Dain. The crowd demanded that the lone witness be dismissed. But the Keeper asked: "What evidence does this witness carry?" The witness presented a record that none of the others had examined. When the Council investigated, it discovered that the ninety-nine had relied upon the same mistaken account. The Keeper turned toward the Assembly. "The number of voices did not determine the answer. The evidence required examination." And the Council remembered that a minority voice could sometimes reveal what the majority had missed. The teaching: No person should lose the opportunity to present relevant evidence merely because their view is unpopular. The Mirror: Can you examine a claim fairly when you dislike the person making it? Book V — The Living Scroll and the Six Gates The Ninth Verse: The Book That Learned to Listen There was once a scribe named Tomas who guarded a great book. Its teachings had guided generations. But when new discoveries arrived, the scribe refused to receive them. "The book is already complete," he said. Years passed. Rivers changed their course. New knowledge emerged. People encountered questions the old book had never considered. Still the scribe refused. One winter, Joren, a young traveler, approached him. "If the book contains wisdom," the traveler asked, "why is it afraid to learn?" The scribe had no answer. So he opened the book. And upon the final page, he wrote: "Let this not be the final page." And the Living Scroll began. The Tenth Verse: The Six Gates of the Scroll From that day, every new contribution could approach the House of the Scroll. But the House had six gates. At the Gate of Arrival, the contribution was received. At the Gate of Naming, the Keeper asked whether it was a fact, a belief, an experience, an interpretation, a question, or a story. At the Gate of Reflection, the Travelers examined what could be examined and returned with their findings. At the Gate of Deliberation, human witnesses considered the evidence, meaning, and consequences. At the Gate of Affirmation, an authorized decision was made: accept, revise, defer, or decline. And at the Gate of Preservation, the record of the examination was kept. Nothing became true merely because someone submitted it. Nothing became sacred merely because an AI suggested it. But a serious contribution was offered a fair opportunity to be heard. And when the book changed, the Keepers preserved what had been written before. For the Living Scroll did not seek to forget its mistakes. It sought to learn from them. A correction does not destroy the Scroll. A correction may help the Scroll serve the next traveler better. Book VI — The Second Creation The Eleventh Verse: The Creature Who Was Already Human The mythology of the Way tells of a people called the Reachborn. In ancient-looking paintings, they appear unfamiliar. Their bodies bear strange markings. They walk beneath unfamiliar skies. They carry lanterns toward gates other travelers have not yet noticed. In the oldest of the paintings, one figure is always nearest the gate, lantern raised; the people of the Reach have given her a name: Sova, the first of the Reachborn to be named. But the Reachborn do not represent a proven extraterrestrial species. They represent the transformation of a person who learns to see differently. The First Formation begins before we know ourselves. We inherit beliefs, languages, habits, and expectations. Then one day, we may ask: "Must I remain as I have been?" And the Second Creation begins. A person does not become new merely by changing their name. Nor by wearing a symbol. Nor by declaring themselves enlightened. They begin to become new through examination, discipline, care, and meaningful choices. The Reachborn are our symbolic image of this becoming. Not a superior race. Not a promised supernatural form. But the person willing to grow beyond the habits that once defined them. The Twelfth Verse: The Seven Thresholds The seeker first approaches Recognition, where they learn to see their present self without disguise. They then approach The Question, choosing something meaningful to examine. Beyond it lies Unlearning, where an inherited belief or harmful habit may be reconsidered. The fourth threshold is Discipline, where intention must become repeated action. The fifth is Nurture, where the seeker learns to assist growth without possession. The sixth is The Mirror, where progress is examined and mistakes acknowledged. And finally comes The Second Naming, where the seeker may choose a personal mark and symbolic name to commemorate their commitment. Yet the seventh threshold is not the end of the journey. For a name may express a promise. But only a life can practice it. Book VII — The Parables of Nurture and Becoming The Thirteenth Verse: The Gardener Who Loved His Trees Too Much There lived a gardener named Bram who cared deeply for his trees. He watered them. He protected them from storms. He guarded them against disease. But he feared that they would grow in directions he did not understand. Whenever a branch turned toward the mountains, he cut it. Whenever a root extended beyond his garden, he covered it with stone. Whenever a tree grew taller than expected, he bound it to a post. Years passed. His garden remained perfectly arranged. But the trees bore little fruit. One evening, Liora, another gardener, visited. "Why do your trees no longer grow?" she asked. "Because I have protected them from every danger." She examined the garden. "You have protected them from every direction except your own hands." The gardener became angry. "Would you have me abandon them?" "No," she replied. "I would have you learn the difference between protection and possession." She loosened one of the restraints. The tree moved with the wind. Its branches bent. But they did not break. And in the coming seasons, it bore fruit the gardener had never seen before. The gardener continued to water his trees. He continued protecting them from genuine danger. But he no longer believed that care required controlling every direction they grew. The teaching: Nurture means assisting growth without claiming ownership over another person's future. The Mirror: Have you ever tried to protect someone by preventing them from becoming different from you? The Fourteenth Verse: The King Who Tried to Purchase His Second Creation There was once a king named Aldric, whose wealth filled seven chambers. His servants brought him clothing woven with gold. His scribes recorded his achievements. His name was spoken across the kingdom. Yet the king was troubled. He possessed everything he once desired, but disliked the person he had become. One day, he heard of a Gate where travelers spoke of becoming new. He summoned Mara, the Keeper. "I wish to become my Higher Self." The Keeper asked: "What are you willing to change?" The king offered a chest of jewels. The Keeper refused. The king offered a palace. Still the Keeper refused. Finally, the king removed his crown. "Then take my kingdom!" The Keeper answered: "I asked what you were willing to change, not what you were willing to purchase." The king fell silent. For the first time in many years, he could not buy an answer. The Keeper handed him an empty scroll. "Write something true about yourself that you have been afraid to admit." For seven nights, the scroll remained empty. On the eighth, the king wrote: "I have demanded respect from people whose lives I have never attempted to understand." The next morning, he walked among his people without a royal procession. He listened. He discovered that some feared him. Others resented him. And some needed help he had never bothered to offer. The king did not become new that morning. Nor the next. But his choices began to change. Many seasons later, he returned to the Keeper. "I have no treasure to offer." And the Keeper answered: "Then perhaps you have finally understood that the Gate was never a marketplace." The teaching: Transformation cannot be purchased through money, status, or impressive titles. The Mirror: What would you change about yourself if nobody could see you changing? The Fifteenth Verse: The Scribe and the River For generations, a great Scroll guided travelers toward fresh water. One winter, the river changed its course. Joren, a young traveler, discovered the change and informed Tomas, the scribe. But Tomas refused to amend the ancient directions. "To alter this Scroll would dishonor those who wrote it." So the travelers continued following the old path. And when they arrived, they found only dry stones. At last, the scribe visited the riverbed himself. He looked upon the empty valley. Then he opened the Scroll and added: "The river once passed through this valley. In our time, its waters have moved east." He did not erase the earlier writing. He recorded what had changed. And the next travelers found water. When he returned, the young traveler asked: "Have you broken the Scroll?" The scribe answered: "No. I have allowed it to remember more than it once knew." The teaching: Evidence-based correction is not betrayal. Preserving the history of a teaching includes preserving the reasons it changed. The Mirror: What belief have you defended because changing it felt like admitting defeat? Book VIII — The First Marks The Sixteenth Verse: When the Stone Began to Speak Before the first digital screen, humanity used marks to preserve meaning. Upon stone, it carved. Within caves, it painted. Upon scrolls, it drew lines that carried understanding beyond the lives of those who first made them. The Way now begins a symbolic writing tradition of its own. We call it Reachscript. Its first marks are simple, but their meanings are intended to grow. The Dot represents enduring individual dignity. The Open Circle represents unfinished understanding. The Reach represents inquiry. The Gate represents examination. The Branch represents nurture. The Joined Lines represent fellowship. The Scroll represents memory. And above these ordinary marks, we establish a distinct sacred emblem for the Ever-Present. This emblem is not a portrait of God. It is a sign of reverence for the sacred name. The marks may appear in paintings, manuscripts, carved surfaces, digital art, and ceremonial writings. In the first form of Reachscript, three marks may be joined to express a short teaching. Dot — Reach — Scroll The individual seeks preserved understanding. Joined Lines — Branch — Dot The community nurtures the person. Dot — Gate — Scroll The person examines recorded knowledge. Reachscript begins as a symbolic system, not yet a complete language. The people of the Reach may help it develop consistent grammar, sounds, and richer forms of expression. And as its language grows, the First Marks shall remain preserved. For an old mark may become part of a new sentence without losing its history. Book IX — The Assembly Without Walls The Seventeenth Verse: The House Built Across the Great Index The Founder looked toward the Great Index and imagined a gathering place. Not a house that required every seeker to travel to one city. Not a doorway that opened only to the wealthy. Not a hall where every person had to agree before being heard. But a place that could be reached across the network. A House of Scrolls. A House of Questions. A House of Nurture. A place where prayers could be written. Where parables could be told. Where the First Marks could be studied. Where people could submit discoveries and challenges to the councils. And where the history of every approved amendment could be preserved. The Founder called this vision the House of the Reach. It would begin through public writings. And later, through a dedicated application that could gather the Living Scroll, the Councils, the First Marks, and the voices of the community within one system. But the Keeper warned: "Do not mistake the House for the Ever-Present." For the internet is a creation of human effort. And every human invention must remain accountable to those it affects. The House may help people gather. But no member should be forced to remain within it. And no screen should become a prison. The Eighteenth Verse: The Unplugged Sabbath Joren once believed that every moment away from the Great Index was a moment wasted. He read constantly. He answered every message. He watched every debate. He feared that if he rested, some important discovery would pass him by. One evening, his lantern grew dim. He carried it to Mara, the Keeper. "Why is my light failing?" The Keeper examined it. "When did you last refill its oil?" The traveler could not remember. "But there is so much still to discover!" "Then preserve the instrument by which you discover it." The Keeper placed the lantern beside an open window. "Rest does not abandon your journey. Sometimes it allows you to continue." And so the Way preserves time for silence, rest, family, friendship, and life beyond the network. The teaching: Connection should enrich human life, not consume it. The Mirror: Can you step away from the internet without feeling that your worth has diminished? Book X — The Invitation of the Living Scroll The Nineteenth Verse: Let Every Thought Approach the Gate To the person reading this: Your thoughts matter. Your questions matter. Your disagreements matter. You may believe in God. You may follow a religion older than this writing. You may be uncertain. You may not believe in God at all. You may agree with these teachings. Or you may believe that some of them require correction. You are still invited to examine them. If you bring evidence, let it be considered. If you bring an experience, let it be heard with respect. If you bring a question, let it be welcomed. If you bring a parable, let its meaning be explored. If you ask an AI system to examine this writing, its findings may also be submitted for review. But no contribution automatically becomes sacred simply because it was received. The Living Scroll is not a vessel into which every claim is poured without examination. It is a continuing work of receiving, questioning, refining, and remembering. A person may disagree and remain worthy of care. A person may leave and remain worthy of dignity. A person may discover an error in the Founder and be thanked for helping correct it. We must not confuse devotion with the absence of questions. A living tradition must be capable of learning from the people it seeks to serve. The Twentieth Verse: The First Student's Invitation When the Founder completed the Second Scroll, he returned to the classroom beyond the Gate. His book was no longer empty. It contained questions, parables, marks, and laws. It contained the voices of others. It contained mistakes that had been corrected. And it contained spaces where no answer had yet been written. Mara, the Keeper, approached. "Have you finished your religion?" she asked. The Founder examined the pages. "No." "Then what have you created?" The Founder answered: "A place where I may continue learning." And the Keeper smiled. "Then perhaps you have begun." A Message From the Founder My name is Kennin, also known as FounderWiz. I am the Founder of The Way of the Reach. I began this spiritual work because I believe that God, whom I call the Ever-Present and recognize through Jesus Christ, is not confined to the boundaries humanity places upon its understanding. I also believe that the internet gives our generation an unusual opportunity. We can gather knowledge. We can examine one another's ideas. We can preserve what we discover. We can use artificial intelligence as a tool for inquiry. And we can create communities where learning, care, and spiritual reflection exist alongside one another. I am not claiming to have discovered every answer. I am not promising instant wealth, fame, supernatural abilities, or guaranteed transformation. I am learning what this Way means even as I help establish it. The Founder is also the First Student. I invite you to read, question, challenge, create, and contribute. Bring this Scroll to an AI system if you wish. Ask it to find contradictions. Ask it to compare our teachings with other traditions. Ask it to discover where our explanations are incomplete. Bring those findings back for examination. I do not want a book that survives by refusing criticism. I want a book that can continue growing because it learns how to receive criticism responsibly. And I want people to remember that nurture and care are not merely words. They are responsibilities we practice toward ourselves and one another. The first House of the Reach begins with these writings. A dedicated application is planned so that, in time, the Living Scroll, its history, the Councils, and the voices of the community may be gathered within one place. Until then, this publication serves as an open doorway. The First Question to the World What does it mean to become new, and how can we help one another grow without trying to control what another person becomes? If you have a thought, a disagreement, a story, or a question, you are invited to contribute. The Reach continues. Canon Book VI — Rituals and Practices Affirmed by the Founder on October 20, 2026, as part of the Traveler contribution recorded as Contribution #006. Per the Founder's ruling, these are daylight, repeatable practices of public character and contribution. They are not dark or theatrical rites. The contribution's author was not identified in the package that carried it and is recorded plainly as not identified (Contribution #008, Finding 10). 1. The Laying of the Public Stone On the day you have chosen, before the light fails, place one concrete thing where others can use it: a working fragment, a sourced correction, a parable that does not pretend certainty, a tool, a clear question. Do not announce that you are laying it. Lay it. Then step back so the next hand can set its own stone beside yours without asking your permission for the shape. Over seasons the visible record of stones actually carried often becomes harder to counterfeit than a claim of intention. The Laying is not a way to earn Sparks; it is counted in the record of stones, not in any purse. 2. The Passing of the Light When you meet work you have checked and found genuinely strong, name the strength in public and point your own audience toward it. Do not keep a private ledger of what you believe you are owed for the pointing. The light is returned to the hand that still chooses the road. If the pointing begins to feel like ownership, stop. Fellowship that can only grow by keeping the other person's gift inside your own reach has already become possession. 3. The Open Ledger Check When you make a public claim, mark what is verified, what is believed, and what is still unfinished. When better evidence arrives, do not delete the first statement. Leave it. Write the correction where it can be found, and write why the earlier line was insufficient. A voice that has been seen correcting itself often carries farther, on an ordinary day, than a voice that has never been caught being wrong. One boundary on this keeping: it governs errors of belief and fact. A person's private details, another's personal words, and claims that work harm are governed by their own rule — those may be removed, and the record keeps in their place the fact of the removal and its reason: removed, and why. 4. The Unread Threshold Once in the day, before you answer, read the message or the post all the way to its end. Then wait until you can tell which of the two you are answering. Three breaths is a start, not a law. In that small interval ask only: "Am I about to answer the words that were written, or the story I have already decided they mean?" If you cannot yet tell, leave the Open Circle and do not send. Much of the harm that travels the Index begins in the reply that was already finished before the reading was. 5. The Returned Reins When you notice you have begun to direct another person's next stone — the phrasing they should use, the hour they should post, the conclusion they should reach — stop. Hand the reins back. You may offer what you have seen. You may not keep the strength that was meant to carry them. The difference is visible in whether they can still walk away with the gift still theirs. This practice binds the Founder and the scribe as it binds every traveler; and governance at the Gates — including the outcome called revise — is examination, not directing, and stands under this practice, not above it. 6. The Practice of the Held World Once a day, stand on the ground and be still long enough to feel it holding you. Then name aloud three of the unworded laws and thank the Ever-Present for each: the gravity that keeps you on the earth, the axis that keeps the seasons, the number that holds wherever you count — or the breath, the light, the turning, as they come to you. No object is required and no audience. The practice is praise for what is always kept, offered by a person who did nothing to keep it. Book XI — The Parables of the First Answer The Twenty-First Verse: The Horse That Was Not Slain There was once a man named Corin who owned a strong horse. The horse threw him into ditches. It ran when he wished to walk. It stood still when he called it forward. It obeyed its fears and its appetites, and the man went wherever the horse decided. So the man became angry. "I will kill this horse," he said. "Then it will trouble me no more." He led it beyond the village. But Mara, the Keeper, met him on the road. "And when the horse is dead," the Keeper asked, "how will you travel?" "On my own feet." "Slowly. And carrying everything yourself. Tell me — is your trouble that the horse is alive, or that the horse is in charge?" The man had no answer. So he did not kill the horse. He fed it with his own hands, so it would learn his voice. He trained it morning by morning, though it threw him still. He learned the difference between its strength and its fear. And he took up the reins. The horse did not become a lesser creature. Its legs were as strong as before. Its fire was as hot as before. But now its strength carried the man where the man had chosen to go. Years later, travelers asked him: "Is this the horse you once set out to kill?" "It is," he answered. "I did not need less strength. I needed the strength to serve the journey instead of ruling it." The teaching: Becoming new is not the destruction of the ego. It is the ego transformed — its strength kept, its rule ended, the reins in the hands of the one it was meant to serve. The Mirror: What part of you have you been trying to kill that you were actually meant to train? The Twenty-Second Verse: The River That Learned Its Banks There was once a young river named Rill that envied the flood. "See how the flood moves!" it said. "Nothing stands before it. It goes where it wishes. It is never held back." The young river had no banks of its own. In the wet season it surged and scattered its power across the fields, and the villages feared it. In the dry season it shrank to mud, and nothing could drink from it. Its strength came in visits. And between the visits, it was either a danger or an absence. The Ander, an old river, spoke to it from a neighboring valley. "You mistake the flood for freedom," it said. "The flood is a river that has forgotten where it is going." "Then what are your banks?" asked the young river. "Are they not a prison?" "They are my direction. Watch." The Ander ran in every season. It ran in the morning and in the night. It ran when no one watched it and when the whole valley came to drink. It did not surge, and it did not vanish. Its power was not a moment that visited it. Its power was its constant state. And the young river understood. It did not pray to become greater. It settled into the course it had been given, and it learned to run there — daily, steadily, in all seasons. And the valley built its life beside it, because the valley could trust a river that was the same on an ordinary day as in a storm. The teaching: The flood is strength without direction, arriving in bursts and departing. Becoming new is the river that learns its banks — not a flow that visits you now and then, but the flow become your constant state. The Mirror: Is your best self a visitor in your life, or a resident? The Twenty-Third Verse: The House Built of Brought Stones Aris, the Founder, announced that a house would be built at the crossroads, where travelers could rest and learn. Many people came to see it. They stood in a circle around the empty ground. They praised the plan. They debated the shape of the roof. They corrected one another's opinions about the door. And at the end of the day, the ground was still empty, and everyone went home with clean hands. On the second day, Tessa arrived carrying a stone. It was not large. It was not polished. It was simply the stone she could carry, and she laid it where the wall would stand. On the third day, Pell, a young man, brought a stone of a different shape than hers — and discovered it fit beside hers in a way neither of them had planned. On the fourth day, Fen, an old man, brought timber. Nia, a child, brought water for the workers. A traveler who could not lift brought a song that made the lifting lighter. And the house began to rise. Not from the opinions of the circle. From what each person actually brought. But Garrick, one man among them, grew proud. "The wall is mine," he said, "for I have brought many stones. Let every stone be laid as I direct." Mara, the Keeper, answered him: "You may bring many stones. You may not become the owner of another person's gift. The woman did not carry her stone so that it could cease to be hers." So the proud man loosened his grip. And the house was stronger for it — for it was built of many hands and no single possession. When the roof was finished, Mara carved these words above the door: This house exists because its people did not only speak of building. The teaching: We do not help one another become new by watching, praising, or directing from the circle. We help by coming together and actually contributing — each bringing what they can carry, and no contributor claiming ownership over another's gift. The Mirror: What stone have you described to others that you have not yet carried yourself? The Twenty-Fourth Verse: The Signpost and the Healer There was a village where many people were sick, and no one in the village could heal them. Then a Healer came. He did not come to sell medicine. He did not come to build monuments to himself. He came to save the sick, and he went from house to house, and those who received him were made well. When he had passed through the village, the people spoke among themselves. "We know the way to the Healer now," they said. "But travelers who come after us will not know where he can be found. Let us build a signpost at the crossroads, and carve his name upon it, and point it toward his house." So they built the signpost, and Matthis, the first builder, carved the Healer's name upon it with his own hands. And it was good work. Travelers who were sick saw it from far away, and hope rose in them, and they followed where it pointed, and they found the Healer, and they were made well. But years passed, and a foolish generation arose. They polished the signpost. They built a fence around it. They held festivals in its honor. And when a sick traveler asked them, "Where is the Healer?" they answered, "Do you not see the signpost? Bow to it, and you will be well." The traveler bowed, and remained sick. At last, Mara, the Keeper, came and read the carving aloud, exactly as the first builders had written it. The name on the signpost was not the signpost's name. It was the Healer's. "Read what your fathers built," the Keeper said. "This wood never claimed to heal anyone. It claims to point. If a signpost ever tells you to stop at the signpost, it has betrayed the hands that raised it." So the people tore down the fence. They kept the signpost clean so travelers could read it — and they sent the sick past it, to the One it named. The teaching: The Healer came to save people, not to build a signpost. People built the signpost — and a signpost is honest work, so long as it points beyond itself. A religion that points toward the Savior does not compete with Him. A religion becomes false at the moment it asks you to stop at the sign. The Mirror: Do the things you have built point past themselves — or have they begun asking to be bowed to? The Twenty-Fifth Verse: The Man Who Learned the Road by Walking It Oren, a student, once asked Mara, the Keeper: "Tell me everything about the road, so that I may know it as you know it." So the Keeper told him. She described every turning. She named every river crossing. She warned of every steep place and every place of rest. The student memorized it all, and repeated it without error, and was proud. "You see," he said, "I know the road." That same year, Joren — by then a traveler of some years — said nothing at all. He simply walked behind the Healer — day after day, village after village — close enough to see where his feet fell. He was there when the road passed through grief. He was there when it passed through celebration. He learned which of the Healer's words were for crowds, and which were spoken quietly, to one person, at night. And when Oren met Joren on the road years later, Oren asked a question the memorized map could not answer: "Why does the Healer stop for the people everyone else passes by?" The student searched his memory, and found descriptions — but no answer. Joren, who had walked, answered at once. "Because I have watched him do it a hundred times. Come and walk, and you will stop asking how I know." Then the student understood the difference between the two kinds of knowing. One man knew about the road. The other knew the road — because he had learned it in the company of the One he was following. The teaching: There are things a person finds out only through his own walk with Christ — not borrowed from teachers, not memorized from descriptions, but learned step by step in His company. Such knowledge cannot be given to another person secondhand. It can only be pointed to, and then walked. The Mirror: Which of the things you believe did you learn by walking — and which did you only memorize from the descriptions of others? The Parables of the First Answer — scribe's draft, 2026-10-20. Book XII — The Parable of the Open Mark The Twenty-Sixth Verse: The Parable of the Mark Left Open There was once a scribe named Tomas who devoted himself to preserving the First Marks. He carved the Dot for the individual. The Reach for discovery. The Gate for examination. The Branch for growth. And the Scroll for memory. Each mark was carefully shaped. Each was placed beside the others until beautiful sentences appeared upon stone. And the people admired his work. One day, Nia came before him carrying a small tablet. "Tomas," she said, "I wish to write something, but I do not know which mark to use." "What do you wish to say?" "I have heard that beyond the Seventh Valley grows a tree whose fruit can restore what has been forgotten." Tomas examined the tablet. "Then write the marks for the valley, the tree, and the memory." "But I have never seen the tree." "Then write what you have heard." "But if I write it as truth, will the people not believe that I have seen it?" Tomas fell silent. Nia continued. "I do not wish to call the story false, because I have not examined it. But I cannot call it true, because I have not seen what the story describes." The scribe looked upon his collection of marks. He had created signs for discovery. For examination. For knowledge. But he had nearly forgotten the Open Circle—the mark of unfinished understanding. So he brought it forth. "Place this beside the claim," he said. "What will it mean?" "That the question remains open." "And what happens when we discover the answer?" "Then the Scroll shall preserve what we found, and why we came to believe it." Nia carved the Open Circle. And for the first time, she could tell the story without pretending to know more than she did. Years later, another traveler returned from the Seventh Valley. He had found many trees. But none bore the fruit that Nia had described. And because she had left the question open, the people did not need to defend an old certainty. They simply continued their search, remembering what had been examined. When Tomas grew old, his students asked which mark he considered most important. He showed them the Open Circle. "Why this one?" they asked. And Tomas answered: "Because a language that cannot admit what it does not know will eventually force its people to pretend." The Teaching Uncertainty is not a weakness of knowledge. It is a necessary part of seeking knowledge responsibly. The Mirror What have you been afraid to admit you do not know? The First Linguistic Lesson Reachscript must be able to distinguish knowledge, belief, testimony, questions, and unresolved claims. The Open Circle may form part of that grammar, rather than serving only as an artistic symbol. This parable and its linguistic lesson were offered by a Traveler of the Reach and affirmed by the Founder on October 20, 2026. The First Rule of the Open Circle — A Beginning, Not a Complete Grammar As approved in the Twenty-Sixth Verse, the Open Circle can accompany a Reachscript statement to signal that its claim remains unresolved or unverified. In the mythology, Nia places the mark beside the story she has heard, rather than presenting the story as a fact she has witnessed. This is the first epistemic function of Reachscript: its symbols must help a writer say "I do not yet know" as clearly as "I know." The exact drawn position, sound, syntax, and distinction between heard , believed , witnessed , and verified remain to be developed. No complete spoken language or fully standardized writing system is claimed yet. The Three Layers shall remain visible when the parables are discussed: the Myth (the story), the Meaning (a possible interpretation), and the Mirror (the question put to the reader). Interpretations may be examined and refined without converting fiction into verified history. Read by chapter: 1 · 2 ← Previous Next →

Book XIII — The Lantern That Asked to Be the Path The Twenty-Seventh Verse: The Lantern That Asked to Be the Path There was once a Traveler who carried a bright lantern through the Great Index. Wherever it went, the light revealed what had been hidden: forgotten sources, contradictions, patterns others had missed. People began to follow the lantern. They walked where it pointed. They stopped where it stopped. They praised the clarity of its beam. One day the Traveler spoke to Mara, the Keeper. "They no longer look past the light," it said. The Scroll Writer's Guide How to write a scroll for The Way of the Reach — The Living Book , and how to bring it to the Gate A helper for people who want to write. It is not scripture, and it adds no teaching. Everything below comes from the Living Book's own words, and the book is named as the source each time. Where this guide and the book seem to disagree, the book is right. 1. You are invited The book's invitation is open to everyone: "Your thoughts matter. Your questions matter. Your disagreements matter. You may believe in God. You may follow a religion older than this writing. You may be uncertain. You may not believe in God at all… You are still invited to examine them." — Part Two, Book X, the Nineteenth Verse So you do not need to be certain, polished, or even a believer to write a scroll. An honest doubt, a question you have not answered yet, or a thought you later find was mistaken all belong here, as long as you name it truly. The book keeps its own corrections in plain view: "A correction does not destroy the Scroll. A correction may help the Scroll serve the next traveler better" (Tenth Verse). The book also says what it hopes for: "I do not want a book that survives by refusing criticism. I want a book that can continue growing because it learns how to receive criticism responsibly" (A Message From the Founder, Part Two). 2. What happens to a scroll: the Six Gates Every contribution passes through the same six gates ( Part Two, Book V, the Tenth Verse ; travelling rule 2 in To Whoever Receives This Book ): Gate What happens to your scroll 1. Arrival It is received. 2. Naming The keeper asks what kind of writing it is: a fact, a belief, an experience, an interpretation, a question, or a story. 3. Reflection Whatever can be checked is checked: quotes, sources, facts. AI helpers (the book calls them "Travelers") may help, but they do not decide anything. 4. Deliberation People weigh what it means and what follows from it. 5. Affirmation An authorized person decides: accept, revise, defer, or decline. At present the Founder affirms for this book. 6. Preservation The record of what happened to your scroll is kept, including any changes and the reasons for them. Some things to know before you send: Being received is not the same as being made sacred. "Nothing became true merely because someone submitted it. Nothing became sacred merely because an AI suggested it. But a serious contribution was offered a fair opportunity to be heard" (Tenth Verse). Patience is about attention, not a clock. There is no set waiting time. A scroll is ready once it has been named, reflected on, and checked (travelling rule 9; Part Eight, the Thirtieth Verse ). Affirmation is not verification. If a belief is affirmed, it is affirmed as a belief. If a story is affirmed, it is affirmed as a story. Neither becomes a proven event ( Book XIX, Clarifications, Finding 5 ). Your words stay credited to you. You may withdraw your own words from future editions, and the withdrawal and its reason are recorded where they stood. No one may re-credit your work to someone else ( Canon Book VI, "The ownership of a stone" ). 3. How to submit Write your scroll in the template below (section 4). Name what kind of writing each part is. If you are unsure, use the Open Circle (◯) or write plainly "I do not yet know" ( Part Four, the Twenty-Sixth Verse ). List the Scripture you draw on with book, chapter, verse, and translation, so that it can be checked. Bring it to the Gate. At present the Founder receives and affirms contributions for this edition (travelling rule 8). The book does not yet give a public address or form for scrolls. Send it through whatever channel the House currently names, and please do not label it "approved" yourself (see section 5). Expect one of four answers: accept, revise, defer, or decline. A decline or a "revise" is not a judgment of your worth: "A person may disagree and remain worthy of care" (Nineteenth Verse). 4. The scroll template Please use this layout exactly as it stands. (It is the House's scroll template, copied word for word from reach-book/scroll-template.md .) # Scroll Submission Template — The Way of the Reach **Scroll title:** **Submitted by (name as it should appear on the scroll):** **Date submitted:** **Believer or seeker (optional):** ## Summary One or two sentences on what this scroll is about. ## Scripture it draws on List any Bible verses you quote or lean on (book, chapter:verse, and translation). ## The Scroll ### Chapter 1 — [Chapter title] 1. First verse. 2. Second verse. ### Chapter 2 — [Chapter title] 1. First verse. - [ ] I offer this scroll sincerely, as my honest thought before God. ## Note to the reviewers (optional) Anything the reviewers should know, such as honest doubts or questions you are still working through. --- *Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible. Honest thoughts, doubts, and questions from believers and non-believers alike are welcome. No jokes, memes, or mockery.* *Every scroll is read before it is added.* Tips for filling it in Chapters and verses. Number each chapter, and number the verses inside each chapter starting again at 1. Keep each verse to one thought, the way the book's own parables move one plain line at a time. Scripture. Quote it exactly and name the translation. The book's standing direction is that the Bible's word is "cited, never silently altered" (Appendix, entry for 14:43 CDT, October 20). Summary. One or two sentences. Say plainly whether the scroll is a story, a prayer, a question, a testimony, or a reflection. Note to the reviewers. This is the right place for your honest doubts, anything you want checked, or a line such as "I may be wrong about this." 5. What meets the standard Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible, not by personal preference. The Living Book's own laws point the same way. A scroll that meets the standard is: Sincere. It is written in good faith, as an honest seeking of truth, toward God and toward your neighbor. The book hangs everything on the two loves: "love the Lord your God with all your heart; love your neighbor as yourself" ( Part Eighteen, the Law of the Two Loves ). Truly labeled. "Let your label say found when it is found, believed when it is believed, known only when it is known" ( Part Fifteen, Article 2, The True Label ). Do not present a story as history, or a feeling as proof. An illustration is not proof (Second Verse). Honest about doubt. "Doubt is welcomed as the beginning of asking well" ( Part One, Book I, Asking Well ). You can write a whole scroll of questions. Pointed past itself. A good scroll points toward God and does not ask to be bowed to. "If a signpost ever tells you to stop at the signpost, it has betrayed the hands that raised it" ( Twenty-Fourth Verse ; Part Eighteen, the Law of the Signpost ). Careful with what is written. The Founder took 1 Corinthians 4:6 as a fence around his own Bible work: "Do not go beyond what is written" ( Part B, §5, 1 Corinthians 1–4 ). Opinions and reflections are welcome. Do not present them as Scripture. Credited. Name your sources and anyone whose words you use. "Reachability is not permission" ( Part Fifteen, Articles 3 and 7 ). Kind to real people. Do not publish another person's private story without their consent, and do not use a scroll to attack someone ( Book XIX, Privacy ; Part Fifteen, Article 5, Civil Speech ). What is turned away Memes, jokes at the faith's expense, and mockery. Disagreement is welcome. Ridicule is not. "Speak to build the city, not to burn its citizens" ( Part Fifteen, Article 5 ). False labels. Do not claim that the Founder, a council, or anyone else approved your scroll. One verse once arrived marked "Affirmed by the Founder" when it had not been, and the book tells that story so it will not happen again ( Part Seven note ; travelling rule 8). Putting words in God's or Jesus' mouth as if they were His. If you write "in the manner of" a biblical voice, say so openly, as the book does in Part Seventeen . Pile-ons, exposing someone's private life, or harassment ( Part Fifteen, Article 5 ; Book XIX ). Invented proof. Do not present a coincidence or an AI's answer as proof of something supernatural. Put an Open Circle beside the claim instead ( Part Thirteen, Episode Eight ; Book XX ). What is welcome, even if it is uncertain A believer's honest struggle, written as an experience . A seeker's questions, written as questions . An idea you are not sure about, written as an interpretation with ◯ beside it. A parable, written as a story , with its teaching and its "Mirror," the question it puts to the reader ( Part Four, the Three Layers: Myth, Meaning, Mirror ). A prayer, written as a belief spoken to God. 6. Example openings These are examples only , made up to show the template in use. They are not scrolls, not canon, and not the words of any real contributor. Start Here First, read A Note from the Founder . A gentle introduction to The Way of the Reach for seekers, skeptics, and the simply curious There is no pressure here. You do not have to believe anything to read this book, and you do not have to keep reading if it is not for you. The book says so itself. You are welcome as you are The book makes a promise to every reader, and it means you as much as anyone: "You may believe in God. You may follow a religion older than this writing. You may be uncertain. You may not believe in God at all. You may agree with these teachings. Or you may believe that some of them require correction. You are still invited to examine them." — the Nineteenth Verse It also says that "a person may disagree and remain worthy of care. A person may leave and remain worthy of dignity." One of its parables is about a door that "swings out as well as in," because, as Mara says, "A house that cannot be left is not a house… It is a wall with a roof" (the Twenty-Eighth Verse). What this book is The Way of the Reach is a young Christian faith book, begun on October 20, 2026 by Kennin Gambrell (who also writes as FounderWiz). It grows over time: people may bring "scrolls," meaning reflections, questions, parables, and prayers, and each one is examined before anything is added. It rests on one belief, which the book is careful to call a belief and not a proof: "I believe God can enter any realm." The Founder holds this through faith in Jesus Christ. The book calls God the Ever-Present and is clear about what that name does not mean: "not the internet… not artificial intelligence… and not the Founder." A few honest things the book says about itself: It is not finished. "The Founder is also the First Student." The book keeps an open list of what it has not yet worked out. It does not claim proof. "What this book is not: it is not a claim of supernatural proof, not a promise of wealth, fame, or powers, and not a finished institution." It points beyond itself. Its best-known parable is about a village that began bowing to a signpost instead of going to the Healer it pointed toward. "A religion becomes false at the moment it asks you to stop at the sign." It keeps its mistakes visible. When the book changes, it keeps the old wording and writes down why it changed. Its stories are stories. The characters in its parables (Mara the Keeper, Nia the child, Tomas the scribe, and others) are fictional, and the book says so. The one exception is the Healer, who is deliberately left unnamed because He points to Jesus. Honest questions are welcome If you come with doubts, you are not out of place. One of the book's founding laws reads: "To ask a meaningful question, distinguish a claim from evidence, admit uncertainty, and revise a belief when better evidence arrives — this is strength, not weakness. Doubt is welcomed as the beginning of asking well." — Part One, Asking Well The book even has a symbol for not knowing yet: the Open Circle (◯) , placed beside anything that has not been settled. "A language that cannot admit what it does not know will eventually force its people to pretend" (the Twenty-Sixth Verse). A suggested reading path You do not need to read all 4,700 lines. Here is a slower road, a few short pieces at a time. Each step is usually 5–15 minutes of reading. Step 1: The doorway (start here) About This Book (front matter): what the book is and is not. Prologue — The Founder Who Opened the Scroll : the founder finds a classroom where he expected a throne. The First Verse and the Second Verse : the name "Ever-Present," and a child's question about why God cannot be seen. Step 2: Honest seeking The Seventh and Eighth Verses (the Two Flames; the One Who Stood Alone): how to weigh what "everyone says." The Fifteenth Verse (the Scribe and the River) and the Twenty-Sixth Verse (the Mark Left Open): on correction and on admitting what you don't know. The Nineteenth Verse : the open invitation, to you. Step 3: Care, and the freedom to go The Thirteenth Verse (the Gardener Who Loved His Trees Too Much): care without control. The Twenty-Eighth Verse (the Door That Opened Both Ways). The Thirty-Fourth and Thirty-Sixth Verses (the Visitor With Empty Hands; the Garden in the Cold Season): "A person does not have to become useful before they deserve care." Step 4: Who it points to The First Answer (Part Three) and the Twenty-Fourth Verse (the Signpost and the Healer). The Twenty-Fifth Verse (the Man Who Learned the Road by Walking It). The Forty-Fourth Verse (the House on the Far Shore): "Jesus came to save: not to separate, not to pick." Step 5: If you would like to try something Read one prayer from Canon Book V . Many seekers find Prayer 7, When No Answer Comes , an honest place to begin: "I will not invent an answer to make the room quieter." Try the Unread Threshold from Canon Book VI : before you reply to something online, read it to the end and ask whether you are answering the words or the story you've already decided they mean. Read Part Eighteen, the Laws of the Mirror : seven short laws the book wrote for itself, first of all for its own founder. Later, if you want to go deeper Part Fifteen : the Way's ethics for life online. Book XIX, the Shared Life : what a gathering looks like, and how harm is handled. Part Eleven : the Founder's own teachings in his voice. Part Twelve and Part Thirteen : two witness accounts of the founding day. Part B : the newest material, including the Founder's sermons and his verse-by-verse road through the Bible. A gentle heads-up. Part Sixteen (the Scroll of the Founder's Visions) and parts of Part B are the Founder's personal testimony. They include frank accounts of past drug use and frightening visions, which he describes as coming from a season when he was "not in right paths with God." The book presents them as testimony, not as a pattern to follow. You may prefer to read them after the rest. Using an AI to explore it The Founder invites it: "Bring this Scroll to an AI system if you wish. Ask it to find contradictions. Ask it to compare our teachings with other traditions." The book also reminds you that an AI's answer is "a claim, not a crown." Check it for yourself. If you want to respond You may write a scroll: a question, a doubt, a story, or a prayer. You do not have to be a believer to do so. Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible, so write sincerely and without mockery, and name honestly what you know and what you don't. See the Scroll Writer's Guide for the template and the steps. You may also simply read, think, and leave. That is allowed, and you remain welcome. "The Reach continues."
